5.text: The shaman Scratching-Woman manifested symptoms of a nature even

6.text: more excitable. He could not sit long in one place, but every little while

7.text: he would jump up with violent gestures. At one time he came to me with

8.text: complaints of a pain he felt “somewhere inside his back,” and I tried to help

9.text: him with a cataplasm. He proved, however, quite unable to endure the

10.text: burning, and began to shout that the fire of Russian shamanism was con-

11.text: suming his whole body: so I had to remove the poultice. Two other Chuk-

12.text: chee who came at the same time with rheumatic complaints, and were treated in

13.text: a similar way, declared only that they felt warm, as in a Russian sweat-bath,

14.text: and requested the application of an extra cataplasm.

15.text: Notwithstanding his youth, Scratching-Woman had already quarreled with

16.text: many neighbors of his own age, and had generally been worsted, because he

17.text: had no peculiar strength or skill at wrestling. His temper was exceedingly

18.text: bad when under the influence of liquor, however slightly. Once, when we

19.text: were sitting in my house and he was on the point of beginning a narrative

20.text: about his “spirits,” another acquaintance of mine and a distant relative of his,

21.text: by name G̣ɪyewteˊhɪn, entered unexpectedly. We saw that he had been

22.text: drinking, having procured the liquor, probably, from a Russian schooner then

23.text: at anchor in the bay near Mariinsky Post. G̣ɪyewteˊhɪn declared that he felt

24.text: lonely, and he also would listen to the words of the shaman.

25.text: Now, Scratching-Woman was exceedly “bashful,” the more so as the

26.text: subject of our talk was concerning his ideas about the “spirits.” Up to this

27.text: time, when acting in the presence of spectators, he had given no explanation

28.text: of his actions or of their significance: therefore he was averse to having an-

29.text: other listener, particularly from his own people. An altercation ensued, and

30.text: G̣ɪyewteˊhɪn threatened to “count the ribs” of Scratching-Woman, should he

31.text: ever again come to his camp. The shaman scowled, and answered with a

32.text: broad allusion to the “spirits” at his command. At last G̣ɪyewteˊhɪn declared

33.text: that he was ready to go if I would treat him to some alcohol. This, of

34.text: course, had been his sole purpose from the beginning. Seeing that the

35.text: shaman was trembling from excitement, and was on the point of pitching

36.text: into his adversary, I hastened to quiet G̣ɪyewteˊhɪn and to send him from

37.text: the house. There could be no question whether to use violence or persuasion,

38.text: since he unhesitatingly declared that, rather than go away without his allow-

39.text: ance of liquor, he would permit himself to be killed, and I gave him full

40.text: credit for the sincerity of his words.¹ When at last he was off with his

41.text: ¹ The passion of this man for strong liquor was something extraordinary, even among the Chukchee.

42.text: He even attempted to steal our bottles in which mice and small birds were preserved, though I made him be-

43.text: lieve that the alcohol in them was poisoned. He would say with great earnestness, “Mice be...! Better take

44.text: me, and immerse me in alcohol in a similar manner. Let me be drowned in strong liquor.”
